title: AI CAD and BIM Case Studies: What Production Evidence Shows
summary: Read AI CAD and BIM deployment case studies with a clear view of the baseline, production scope, review effort, exceptions, and measured outcomes.
body_markdown:
If you're looking for evidence that AI agents are doing real CAD and BIM production work, the short answer is that the public sources we reviewed don't offer much yet. There are useful customer stories about generative design, conference talks about maintaining automation, and recordings of agents carrying out modeling tasks. They describe different kinds of work. Measured case studies of an agent producing native drawings or models on live projects, with numbers behind them, are rare. The examples below show what each source can tell you about using AI on a project.


## AI CAD BIM vendors production deployment case studies


Start by asking what technology a case study actually describes. Traditional scripted automation, AI-assisted programming, concept generation and conversational model editing all get marketed as "AI", and each one answers a different question for a firm deciding what to buy.


### RBA Architects: faster site planning with TestFit


[TestFit's account of RBA Architects](https://www.testfit.io/blog/10-customers-that-shaped-10-years-of-testfit) describes a specific production bottleneck: preparing a site plan in AutoCAD, then building the massing in Revit. The vendor reports that this previously took 20–30 hours for the plan and another 30–40 for the massing, compared with 4–6 hours in TestFit. These are reported customer results, not measurements we independently verified.


The useful detail is the workflow that changed. A feasibility tool let the architects explore layouts without rebuilding the plan and massing separately each time. That is relevant if your team spends its time on site options. It doesn't establish how a conversational agent will update door parameters or issue construction sheets inside Revit. The result belongs to the task that was measured.


### Autodesk University: AI helping maintain existing automation


Another example is an[Autodesk University 2026 session](https://www.autodesk.com/autodesk-university/class/Beyond-the-Foundation-Scaling-10-Years-of-Legacy-Code-for-the-Next-Generation-2026) on scaling a decade of legacy code. It describes using AI to help modernize longstanding AutoCAD and Civil 3D code. That's a real production problem, and an important one for any office sitting on a library of aging routines. The session shows that AI can help a team maintain its automation. It doesn't show a commercial agent drafting without supervision, and reading it that way takes it beyond what it describes.


## What a vendor recording can show you


ArchiLabs publishes recordings of Desktop working in Revit, made with public source documents and prepared models. In one, a manufacturer's equipment PDF becomes a native Revit family placed in a project. The recording notes that dimensions the PDF didn't give were approximated and that the waiting periods were edited out. Another shows architectural PDF plans becoming a native Revit building, follow-up corrections included.


Recordings like these are good for seeing what goes in, how you work with the agent, and what comes out: a native family or model you can open and edit. What they can't show is how the workflow holds up after weeks of use, who owns it on a project, and how much effort it takes to keep it running. A deployment case study is supposed to answer those questions, and much of the public evidence we reviewed leaves them open.


## What separates a deployment story from a demo


Three things usually set an account of real use apart from a well-made demo.


The first is a clear picture of how the work was done before. Suppose a case study says AI halved sheet production time. That could mean very different things depending on what "sheet production" covered. Generating view names is a small job. Creating sheets, placing views, reviewing layouts and exporting the package is a large one. The percentage can't be compared with anything until the study says which job it measured, and whether the "before" time was actually measured or estimated by an experienced team member.


The second is what happened to the exceptions. Real projects have mismatched IDs, missing source fields and office standards the tool has never seen. A deployment story should say how often those cases came up and who fixed them. A study that shows only successful runs is a set of good examples. They're worth seeing, but they tell you little about how much of the work still needed a person.


The third is whether the workflow outlasted the person who built it. Automation often works well for its author. What matters is whether a second person could run it, how they learned it, and what happened on the next project. Did the team reuse its mappings and standards, or start over? The answer tells you more about the ongoing cost than any first-run result. Our guide to the[Revit automation review handoff package](https://archilabs.ai/posts/revit-automation-review-handoff-package) covers what someone else needs in order to pick up an automated task and keep it going.


## Watching, then testing


Until more measured case studies are published, the most honest evidence is the kind you can watch and then try yourself. The recordings on the[ArchiLabs Desktop page](https://archilabs.ai/desktop) show what goes in and what comes out in native Revit. Desktop works on your own files in Revit 2023 through 2027, so running a recurring task from one of your current projects will show you whether those results hold up in your office.
